newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Sympathy but little forgiveness for Kim Young-sam.
newsitem.headline: Sympathy but little forgiveness for Kim Young-sam.

text.p: The spectacle of a once-popular president apologising humbly to the nation drew some sympathy, but little forgiveness, from ordinary South Koreans on Tuesday.

With an abject display of contrition, Kim Young-sam had hoped to redeem his reputation and rescue his fading presidency. But there was little immediate sign his television address had convinced a sceptical public.
"His speech was sincere, but it can't make up for his four years of failures," said Oh Kil-hwan, 45, a trader, after watching the live broadcast.
Kim was a model penitent, following in a long Korean tradition of leaders appealing for understanding for their shortcomings in office.
According to custom, he kept his eyes downcast, his voice hushed and his manner grave.
"We will watch him in his last year as president, but I don't think he will be able to correct the past," Oh said.
Crowds gathered in front of television screens at Seoul Railway Station and other public places to watch Kim's last-ditch efforts to rescue his final year in office.
"All you ever do is apologise. What good is that!", one man yelled.

It was not the first time Kim has admitted mistakes, but he went further than ever before in trying to make amends, reflecting his precipitous drop in popularity polls. One recent survey gave him a 10 percent approval rating.

Tuesday marked Kim's fourth anniversary in office. Now white-haired and visibly ageing, Kim was swept to power pledging to wipe out corruption -- what many exasperated South Koreans call the "Korean disease".
Yet in the latest scandal to rock his administration, three of his close aides have been arrested and are in custody over loans to the failed Hanbo Steel Co.

Some Koreans were also scandalised by the forced passage of a controversial new labour law, a practice reminiscent of the days when South Korea was ruled by a military strongman and Kim, then a leading dissident, loudly denounced such abuse of power.
"He gave us hope at the beginning, now he makes us wonder if he himself is not corrupt," said one 59-year-old woman, who asked not to be named.

Kim's last television appearance in January when he vigorously defended the new labour law was a public relations disaster, convincing many people that the president had became autocratic and uncaring.
Kim's single term expires in February 1998 but, to protect himself after he leaves office, he is anxious to install a protege in the presidential Blue House.
"What will an apology do?" asked farmer Hwang Yoon-sul. "Kim Young-sam is the worst ever dictator of Korea."
Not everyone criticised the president. Kim Jung-kil, a retired real estate agent, laid the blame on Kim's aides.
"He made an apology. What more could the Korean people want?" he said.
"I think President Kim's aides are corrupt and are misleading the president," said Kim. "History will show the president is innocent. After all, he has fought all his life for democracy."
